choices: Real loyalty, even when it feels a little scary
It shows nothing meaningful at all
quiz.explanation: Telling a group 'that's not cool, leave them alone' when they're teasing your friend takes courage, but shows real loyalty. Speaking up, even briefly, can mean everything to them.

quiz.question: What does real listening look like?
choices: Asking follow-up questions and remembering details
Waiting for your turn to talk about yourself
quiz.explanation: A friend who remembers you had a big test and asks how it went, without being reminded, is really listening. That attention, instead of waiting to talk, makes someone feel cared about.

quiz.question: What can help you notice when a friend might be struggling, even if they haven't said anything?
choices: Noticing changes like them going quiet or seeming off
Assuming everything is always fine
quiz.explanation: Sometimes a friend won't say directly that something's wrong, so noticing them go quiet or seem off is an important clue. Gently checking in can matter more than you'd think.

quiz.question: What's the best way to help a friend who's going through something hard?
choices: Ask what they actually need instead of deciding for them
Take over and fix everything your own way
quiz.explanation: Asking a struggling friend what they actually need, instead of deciding for them, respects how they're feeling. Sometimes they just want someone to listen, not someone to fix it.

quiz.question: How can you stand up for a friend online?
choices: Commenting something supportive if they're being mocked
Staying silent because it's not happening in person
quiz.explanation: Commenting something supportive if a friend is mocked in a group chat matters just as much as standing up for them in person. Online teasing can feel just as hurtful.

quiz.question: Why is it meaningful to check in with a friend the next day about something hard?
choices: It shows you cared beyond just that moment
It doesn't matter once the moment has passed
quiz.explanation: Following up the next day about something hard, like a rough test or a fight at home, shows your care wasn't just a one-time thing. That extra step means a lot.

quiz.question: How does inclusion apply to group chats?
choices: Remembering to add someone who might otherwise be left out
Group chats don't really matter for inclusion
quiz.explanation: Remembering to add someone to a group chat who might otherwise be left out matters just as much as inviting them in person. A lot of socializing now happens online.

quiz.question: What's a small action that can make a big difference for someone who's often left out?
choices: Inviting them along even once
Waiting for someone else to include them first
quiz.explanation: Inviting someone along even just once, like to a group project or a hangout, can change how included they feel for a long time. They might never say it out loud, but it matters.

quiz.question: What's a sign that you're truly listening rather than just waiting to talk?
choices: Remembering details they've told you before
Thinking about your own response the whole time
quiz.explanation: Remembering details a friend shared before, like a worry they mentioned last week, shows you were genuinely paying attention. That's different from just waiting for a pause to talk about yourself.

slides.title: Dealing with jealousy
slides.text: Feeling a little jealous when a friend does something great isn't unusual, but acting on that jealousy can hurt the friendship — noticing the feeling and choosing kindness anyway matters. For example, feeling a twinge of jealousy when a friend makes a team you didn't, but still congratulating them sincerely, protects the friendship even though the feeling is uncomfortable.

slides.title: Friendships that drift apart
slides.text: Sometimes friends grow apart naturally as interests change, and that's a normal part of growing up, not something that means you did anything wrong. For example, a childhood best friend moving toward different hobbies and a different friend group over a couple of years doesn't mean either of you failed at friendship — people just change.

slides.title: Online friendships
slides.text: Online friendships can feel meaningful, but you still need to protect private information. Someone being friendly in a game or app does not mean you should share your full name, school, address, passwords, or live location. If anything feels strange or secretive, tell a trusted adult.

slides.title: Saying sorry and meaning it
slides.text: A real apology isn't just about avoiding an awkward silence — it means acknowledging what you did, how it affected your friend, and actually changing the behavior going forward. For example, saying 'I'm sorry I canceled last minute again, I'll give you more notice next time' means a lot more than a quick, vague 'my bad.'

slides.title: When a friendship feels one-sided
slides.text: Noticing if you're always the one reaching out or making plans is worth paying attention to, since healthy friendships usually involve effort from both sides.

slides.title: Setting a boundary with a friend
slides.text: It's okay to tell a friend that something they do bothers you, even if it feels uncomfortable to bring up, because a caring friend should be willing to hear you.

slides.title: Comparing yourself to friends
slides.text: Comparing your grades, looks, or achievements to a friend's can quietly chip away at the friendship, so noticing when you're doing it is the first step to letting it go.

slides.title: Meeting online friends safely
slides.text: Never arrange to meet an online friend by yourself. If meeting is ever considered, involve a trusted adult from the beginning and meet only in a safe, public setting with adult supervision.

slides.title: Group chat drama
slides.text: Misunderstandings happen easily over text since tone is hard to read, so it's often better to talk through a disagreement in person or by call rather than in a long group chat argument.

slides.title: Apologizing without over-explaining
slides.text: A lengthy apology that focuses on justifying yourself can feel less sincere than a short, honest one that focuses on how the other person feels.

quiz.question: What's a healthy way to handle jealousy toward a friend's success?
choices: Notice the feeling but choose to be kind and supportive anyway
Let the jealousy control how you treat them
quiz.explanation: Feeling a twinge of jealousy when a friend makes a team you didn't is normal, but congratulating them sincerely anyway protects the friendship. Noticing the feeling without acting mean on it is the healthier choice.

quiz.question: What does it mean if you and a childhood friend grow apart?
choices: It's a normal part of growing up, not necessarily anyone's fault
It always means someone did something wrong
quiz.explanation: A childhood best friend drifting toward different hobbies and a new friend group over a couple of years doesn't mean either of you failed. People naturally change as they grow up, and that's okay.

quiz.question: What's an important caution with online friendships?
choices: Being careful about sharing personal details with people you've never met
There's no need to be careful about anything online
quiz.explanation: Having a great time playing an online game with someone doesn't mean it's safe to share your home address or school name with them. Online friendships can be real, but personal details deserve extra caution.

quiz.question: What makes an apology mean more than just avoiding awkwardness?
choices: Acknowledging what happened and actually changing your behavior
Saying 'my bad' quickly and moving on
quiz.explanation: Saying 'I'm sorry I canceled last minute again, I'll give you more notice next time' means far more than a quick, vague 'my bad.' A real apology names what happened and shows you'll actually change.

quiz.question: What's worth paying attention to in a friendship?
choices: Whether you're always the one reaching out
Only how much fun you have together
quiz.explanation: Noticing if you're always the one texting first or planning the hangout is worth watching, since healthy friendships usually involve effort from both sides. One person carrying all the effort can quietly wear a friendship down.

quiz.question: Is it okay to tell a friend something they do bothers you?
choices: Yes, a real friend will want to know
No, you should never bring up small annoyances
quiz.explanation: Telling a friend that something they do, like showing up late every time, bothers you can feel uncomfortable to bring up. A caring friend should be open to hearing that something is bothering you.

quiz.question: What can chip away at a friendship over time?
choices: Constantly comparing yourself to your friend
Celebrating your friend's achievements
quiz.explanation: Constantly comparing your grades or looks to a friend's can quietly build resentment, even if you never say anything out loud. Noticing when you're doing it is the first step to letting it go.

quiz.question: What's an important safety step with an online friend?
choices: Never agreeing to meet in person without a trusted adult knowing
Meeting up alone as soon as they ask
quiz.explanation: Never agreeing to meet an online friend in person without telling a trusted adult first is an important safety rule. Even a friendship that feels completely genuine deserves that extra caution.

quiz.question: Why can misunderstandings happen easily in a group chat?
choices: Tone is hard to read over text
Text always makes feelings perfectly clear
quiz.explanation: A joke that would land fine in person can sound harsh in a text, because tone and facial expressions get lost. That's why a real conversation or call often clears things up faster.

quiz.question: What can make an apology feel less sincere?
choices: A long explanation that focuses on justifying yourself
A short apology that focuses on the other person's feelings
quiz.explanation: A lengthy apology that spends most of its time explaining why you did it can feel more like an excuse than remorse. A short, honest apology that focuses on the other person's feelings usually lands better.

slides.title: Authentic vs. surface-level friendships
slides.text: Some friendships stay surface-level — fun but not deep — while others grow into real trust over time; both have their place, but knowing the difference helps you invest your energy well. For example, someone you only ever talk to about school gossip is a different kind of friend than someone you'd call at late at night with a real problem — both are valid, but they're not the same.

slides.title: Mutual respect and boundaries
slides.text: A healthy friendship respects that both people have limits — like needing space sometimes, or not wanting to discuss certain topics — without taking it personally. For example, a friend saying 'I need some space this weekend' isn't a rejection; respecting that request without guilt-tripping them is part of a mature friendship.

slides.title: Vulnerability deepens friendship
slides.text: Sharing something real—such as a worry, fear, or honest opinion—can deepen a friendship when enough trust already exists. Start with smaller things and notice whether the other person responds with care and respects your privacy before sharing more personal information.

slides.title: Being reliable under pressure
slides.text: A real test of friendship is whether you show up for someone even when it's inconvenient or a little uncomfortable, not just when it's easy. For example, going to support a friend at a hard event, even though you'd rather be somewhere else that night, is the kind of reliability that real friendships are built on.

slides.title: Different friends for different needs
slides.text: It's normal, and healthy, to have one friend you go to for deep conversations and another you mostly just have fun with; expecting a single person to meet every one of your needs often puts too much pressure on that friendship.

slides.title: Trust is built gradually, not all at once
slides.text: Sharing something vulnerable too fast with someone you barely know can feel like a shortcut to closeness, but trust earned slowly through consistent small moments tends to hold up better over time.

slides.title: You don't owe anyone unconditional access to you
slides.text: Being a good friend doesn't mean being available every single time someone wants your attention; protecting some of your own time and energy is part of a sustainable friendship, not a betrayal of it.

slides.title: Reciprocity in friendship
slides.text: A healthy friendship usually has a rough balance of give and take over time, even if it's not perfectly even week to week; a long-term pattern of one-sided effort is worth taking seriously.

slides.title: Friendship and self-respect
slides.text: Respecting yourself within a friendship means being willing to voice disagreement or discomfort, rather than always going along with what a friend wants just to avoid conflict.

slides.title: Let closeness grow with trust
slides.text: You do not have to share your most personal thoughts with someone just because you get along quickly. It is okay to let trust build step by step as you see how the other person handles small confidences, disagreements, and boundaries.

quiz.question: What's the difference between a surface-level and a deep friendship?
choices: Depth of trust and how much you'd share with them
There's no real difference at all
quiz.explanation: A friend you only talk to about school gossip is different from one you'd call at late at night with a real problem, and both kinds are valid. Knowing which is which helps you invest your energy where it fits.

quiz.question: What does respecting a friend's boundaries look like?
choices: Accepting their limits, like needing space, without guilt-tripping them
Taking any boundary personally as a rejection
quiz.explanation: A friend saying 'I need some space this weekend' isn't a rejection, it's just a limit. Respecting that without guilt-tripping them is part of what makes a friendship feel safe and mature.

quiz.question: Why does sharing something vulnerable often deepen a friendship?
choices: It builds real trust, even though it feels risky
Vulnerability always pushes friends away
quiz.explanation: Admitting to a friend that you're actually nervous about a decision, instead of pretending everything's fine, feels risky but usually brings you closer. Genuine openness often turns a casual friendship into one you can really lean on.

quiz.question: What's a true test of friendship reliability?
choices: Showing up for someone even when it's inconvenient
Only being there when it's easy and convenient
quiz.explanation: Anyone can be a good friend when it's easy, but showing up at a hard event, even when you'd rather be elsewhere, is the real test. That kind of reliability is what real friendships get built on.

quiz.question: Is it healthy to rely on different friends for different needs?
choices: Yes, expecting one friend to meet every need puts too much pressure on that friendship
No, you should have exactly one friend who meets all your needs
quiz.explanation: It's completely normal to have one friend for deep conversations and another you mostly just have fun with. Expecting a single person to be everything for you puts more pressure on that friendship than it can usually hold.

quiz.question: How does trust usually hold up best in a friendship?
choices: When it's earned slowly through consistent small moments
When it's built instantly by sharing everything right away
quiz.explanation: Sharing something deeply personal with someone you barely know can feel like a shortcut to closeness, but it often isn't earned yet. Trust built gradually through consistent small moments tends to hold up much better.

quiz.question: Does being a good friend mean always being available?
choices: No, protecting some of your own time and energy is healthy
Yes, a good friend must always be available
quiz.explanation: Being a good friend doesn't mean dropping everything every time someone wants your attention. Protecting some of your own time and energy is part of a sustainable friendship, not a betrayal of it.

quiz.question: What's worth paying attention to in a friendship's balance?
choices: A long-term pattern of one-sided effort
Whether every single week is perfectly equal
quiz.explanation: A single week where you did more of the reaching out doesn't mean much on its own. It's a long-term pattern, like always being the one to text first for months, that's actually worth noticing.

quiz.question: What does self-respect look like within a friendship?
choices: Being willing to voice disagreement or discomfort
Always going along with a friend to avoid conflict
quiz.explanation: Respecting yourself in a friendship means being willing to say 'actually, I don't agree' instead of always going along to avoid friction. A friendship that only works when you suppress your opinions isn't fully honest.

quiz.question: Why might sharing something vulnerable too quickly with someone you barely know backfire?
choices: It can feel like a shortcut to closeness that hasn't actually been earned
It always guarantees instant closeness
quiz.explanation: Telling someone you just met your deepest worries can feel bonding in the moment, but that closeness hasn't actually been built yet. Trust usually needs time and small proven moments first.

slides.title: Repairing a friendship after conflict
slides.text: Not every disagreement has to end a friendship — a real conversation about what happened, without rehashing every old grievance, can often repair things. For example, having one honest, calm conversation about a specific fight — instead of avoiding each other for weeks — often clears the air faster than either person expects.

slides.title: Recognizing toxic patterns
slides.text: Instead of judging a friendship from one bad moment, look for repeated patterns: frequent put-downs, pressure, dishonesty, using you only when they need something, or leaving you consistently anxious or drained. Repeated behavior matters more than one difficult day.

slides.title: Resisting pressure to exclude someone
slides.text: Peer pressure to leave someone out or join in on unkind behavior can be hard to resist, but choosing not to participate — even quietly — matters. For example, not joining in when a group starts excluding or mocking someone, even if you don't openly object, is a meaningful choice not to add to the harm.

slides.title: Handling jealousy without damaging trust
slides.text: Feeling a flicker of jealousy when a friend succeeds at something you wanted for yourself is normal — the difference between a healthy friendship and a strained one is often what you do with that feeling. For example, privately acknowledging you feel a little envious, while still congratulating your friend sincerely, keeps the friendship intact instead of letting an unspoken resentment quietly build up.

slides.title: The difference between a bad moment and a bad pattern
slides.text: Everyone has an off day, including good friends, so one frustrating interaction doesn't define a friendship; it's the pattern over time, not a single incident, that matters most.

slides.title: When to step back from a friendship
slides.text: It can be reasonable to create distance when a friendship repeatedly feels unsafe, disrespectful, controlling, or exhausting and honest conversations do not improve things. Stepping back can mean less contact, clearer boundaries, or ending the friendship if needed.

slides.title: Manipulation vs. honest disagreement
slides.text: There's a real difference between a friend honestly disagreeing with you and a friend using guilt, silent treatment, or threats to end the friendship to get their way; learning to notice that difference protects you.

slides.title: Addressing conflict directly vs. through others
slides.text: Venting about a disagreement to a mutual friend, instead of talking to the person involved, often makes a conflict worse and drags other people into something that isn't theirs.

slides.title: Apologizing for your part, even in a mutual conflict
slides.text: Most conflicts involve some contribution from both sides, so being willing to own your specific part, even if the other person also did something wrong, tends to resolve things faster.

slides.title: Look for patterns, not labels
slides.text: One rude comment or bad day does not automatically define a whole friendship. Pay attention to repeated behavior over time—how often problems happen, whether the person takes responsibility, and whether things improve after you talk about them.

quiz.question: What often helps repair a friendship after a conflict?
choices: An honest, calm conversation about what happened
Avoiding each other indefinitely
quiz.explanation: One honest, calm conversation about a specific fight, instead of avoiding each other for weeks, often clears the air faster than either person expects. Naming what happened, without dragging up old grievances, gives the friendship room to move forward.

quiz.question: What's a sign of a potentially toxic friendship pattern?
choices: Consistently feeling drained or worse after spending time with them
Feeling happy and supported most of the time
quiz.explanation: Noticing that you consistently feel drained or anxious after spending time with a specific person, rather than just having one bad day, is worth taking seriously. A pattern like that says more than any single hangout does.

quiz.question: What's a meaningful way to resist pressure to exclude someone?
choices: Simply not joining in, even quietly
Joining in so you're not the odd one out
quiz.explanation: Not joining in when a group starts excluding or mocking someone, even if you don't openly object, is a real choice not to add to the harm. It takes quiet courage to step back from something everyone else is doing.

quiz.question: What's the healthy way to handle jealousy toward a friend's success?
choices: Acknowledge the feeling privately, but still support them sincerely
Let the resentment build up silently
quiz.explanation: Privately admitting you feel a little envious when a friend succeeds, while still congratulating them sincerely, keeps the friendship intact. Letting that feeling stay unspoken is what tends to cause real damage.

quiz.question: What matters more in judging a friendship?
choices: The overall pattern over time, not a single off day
Any one frustrating interaction, no matter how rare
quiz.explanation: Everyone has an off day, even good friends, so one frustrating interaction doesn't define a whole friendship. It's the pattern over time that actually tells you something.

quiz.question: Is it okay to distance yourself from a consistently stressful friendship?
choices: Yes, it's a legitimate choice, not a failure
No, you should never step back from any friendship
quiz.explanation: Stepping back from a friendship that's become a consistent source of stress, rather than support, isn't a failure on your part. Choosing to protect your own wellbeing is a legitimate, healthy decision.

quiz.question: What's a sign of manipulation rather than honest disagreement?
choices: Using guilt or threats to end the friendship to get their way
Calmly explaining why they see things differently
quiz.explanation: A friend calmly explaining why they see something differently is honest disagreement. A friend using guilt or threats to get what they want is manipulation, and learning to tell the two apart protects you.

quiz.question: What often makes a conflict worse?
choices: Venting to a mutual friend instead of talking to the person involved
Talking directly to the person you disagree with
quiz.explanation: Venting about a disagreement to a mutual friend, instead of talking to the person actually involved, often makes the conflict worse. It drags other people into something that isn't theirs.

quiz.question: What tends to resolve a mutual conflict faster?
choices: Being willing to own your specific part in it
Waiting for the other person to apologize first
quiz.explanation: Most conflicts involve some contribution from both sides, so owning your specific part, even if the other person also did something wrong, helps break the standoff. Waiting for them to go first often just leaves both people stuck.

quiz.question: What's a healthier response to noticing a toxic pattern in a friendship, over just one bad day?
choices: Taking the repeated pattern seriously
Dismissing it since everyone has bad days sometimes
quiz.explanation: Everyone has an off day, so a single bad moment doesn't need to be a big deal. But a repeated pattern, like always feeling worse after seeing someone, deserves to be taken seriously.

slides.title: Long-distance friendships
slides.text: Friendships can survive moving away or going to different schools, but they usually need more intentional effort — a call, a message, a visit — since you won't just run into each other anymore. For example, scheduling a regular video call with a friend who moved away, instead of hoping you'll naturally stay in touch, keeps a long-distance friendship genuinely alive.

slides.title: Growing in different directions
slides.text: As people figure out who they are during the teen years, some friendships naturally fade — that's a normal part of growing, not a personal failure on either side. For example, two friends who were inseparable in middle school discovering very different interests and friend groups by the end of high school is a common, normal part of growing up.

slides.title: Being present: the power of good listening
slides.text: Really listening — putting your phone down, asking questions, and not planning your response while the other person is still talking — is one of the most underrated ways to deepen a friendship. For example, a friend who remembers a hard conversation from weeks ago and checks in about it, unprompted, is showing a kind of attentiveness that most casual friendships never reach.

slides.title: Including someone who's new or on the outside
slides.text: Actively including someone who's new, quiet, or often left on the edge of a group takes a small amount of effort but can change how they experience an entire year. For example, texting someone you don't know well to invite them along, instead of assuming they'll ask to join, is a simple way to make a group feel more open.

slides.title: Making friends outside your usual circle
slides.text: As your interests and identity keep developing through your teen years, some of your best friendships might come from outside your usual friend group — a club, a job, or a shared interest online. For example, a genuine friendship with someone from a completely different social circle can offer a perspective and support that your closer, more similar friends might not.

slides.title: Staying friends across big life changes
slides.text: Not just physical distance, but changes like different schools after graduation, new jobs, or different life paths can strain a friendship; the friendships that last are often the ones both people actively choose to keep investing in.

slides.title: Making the first move
slides.text: Reaching out first, even though it can feel vulnerable to be the one who initiates, is often exactly what a fading friendship needs to stay alive.

slides.title: Diversifying your friend group by choice
slides.text: Actively seeking out friends with different backgrounds or perspectives than your own tends to broaden how you see the world, not just add more people to your contact list.

slides.title: Letting go without bitterness
slides.text: When a friendship fades naturally, it's possible to feel grateful for what it was without needing to stay close forever or view the ending as a failure.

slides.title: Friendships need shared effort
slides.text: Staying connected usually works best when both people sometimes reach out, make plans, and show interest in each other's lives. The effort will not be perfectly equal every week, but over time it should not feel like only one person is carrying the friendship.

quiz.question: What helps long-distance friendships survive?
choices: Intentional effort, like calls, messages, or visits
Assuming it'll stay strong with zero effort
quiz.explanation: Scheduling a regular video call with a friend who moved away, instead of hoping you'll naturally stay in touch, keeps a long-distance friendship genuinely alive. Without running into each other by chance anymore, staying close takes real effort.

quiz.question: Why might friends drift apart during the teen years?
choices: People naturally grow and change, which is a normal part of growing up
It always means someone did something wrong
quiz.explanation: Two friends who were inseparable in middle school can end up with very different interests by the end of high school, and that's common. As people figure out who they are, some friendships naturally fade without it being anyone's fault.

quiz.question: What does really listening to a friend look like?
choices: Putting your phone down and asking questions instead of planning your reply
Waiting for your turn to talk about yourself
quiz.explanation: A friend who remembers a hard conversation from weeks ago and checks in about it, unprompted, is showing real attentiveness. Putting your phone down and truly focusing is what most casual friendships never quite reach.

quiz.question: Why is it worth making friends outside your usual circle?
choices: It can offer perspectives your closer friends might not
It's pointless since only your close friends matter
quiz.explanation: A genuine friendship with someone from a completely different social circle, like a job or an online community, can offer a perspective your closer friends might not have. Stepping outside your usual group broadens how you see things.

quiz.question: What can make a meaningful difference for someone who's new or on the outside of a group?
choices: Actively including them, like texting to invite them along
Assuming they'll ask to join if they want to
quiz.explanation: Texting someone you don't know well to invite them along, instead of assuming they'll ask to join, takes a small amount of effort. That one gesture can change how included they feel for a long time.

quiz.question: What helps friendships survive big life changes, like graduating or moving for a job?
choices: Both people actively choosing to keep investing in it
Assuming the friendship will continue with no effort
quiz.explanation: Different schools, new jobs, or different life paths can naturally strain a friendship over time. The friendships that last are the ones where both people actively choose to keep investing in them.

quiz.question: Why does reaching out first matter for a fading friendship?
choices: It's often exactly what the friendship needs to stay alive
It never makes any real difference
quiz.explanation: Being the one to reach out first, even though it can feel vulnerable, is often exactly what a fading friendship needs to stay alive. Someone has to make the first move, and it can just as easily be you.

quiz.question: What's a benefit of seeking out friends with different backgrounds or perspectives?
choices: It broadens how you see the world
It has no real effect beyond adding more contacts
quiz.explanation: Actively seeking out friends with different backgrounds does more than add names to your contact list. It genuinely broadens how you understand the world in a way that similar friends often can't.

quiz.question: How can you think about a friendship that fades naturally?
choices: Feel grateful for what it was, without viewing it as a failure
You must always view a faded friendship as a failure
quiz.explanation: When a friendship fades naturally, it's possible to feel genuinely grateful for what it was without needing to stay close forever. Not every ending is a failure — some friendships simply belonged to a season of life.

quiz.question: What does being present with a friend involve?
choices: Putting your phone down and really focusing on them
Half-listening while doing something else
quiz.explanation: Being present means putting your phone down and giving a friend your full attention, not just being in the same room. That kind of focus is what makes someone feel truly heard.
